chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Hanan ibn Sadeer, from his father, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him about the harm from his neighbour. So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Be patient.' Then he came to him a second time, so the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Be patient.' Then he returned to him and complained to him for the third time. So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to the man who complained: 'When the people are commuting to the Friday prayer, take out your belongings to the road until those who are going to the Friday prayer see you. So when they ask you, inform them.' He said: 'He did so, and his harming neighbour came to him and said to him, 'Return your belongings, and by Allah, I will not repeat (harming you).'
ai.seo_question: How did the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) advise resolving neighbourly disputes?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the nuanced Shia approach to neighborly rights, balancing initial forbearance with pragmatic action when patience fails. The Prophet’s instruction to display belongings during the Friday commute leverages the social visibility of the congregation to create a public witness for the dispute, a method consistent with early Islamic community dynamics. This narrative underscores that while patience is virtuous, it is not an obligation to endure persistent harm indefinitely, reflecting the principle of 'la darar wa la dirar' (no harm and no reciprocating harm).
